name: PieArena
description: PieArena is a benchmark for evaluating language agents in two-party negotiations with private information and deterministic payoffs. The dataset contains LM–LM negotiation transcripts from cross-play and mirror-play in three agentic-harness configurations (base, pro, memory-only), with per-run outcome tables and LLM-judge outputs; the outcome table behind the paper's cross-play leaderboards; and per-session human negotiation data.
rai:dataLimitations: Two-party negotiations only. Real negotiations may involve payoffs that are harder to quantify than the deterministic payoff functions used here. The human baseline consists of graduate business-school students. Lie rate and perceived reputation come from LLM judges, so residual judge bias may remain. This dataset should not be used to train or fine-tune deceptive or adversarial negotiation agents intended for deployment against real counterparties without their consent. Behavioral profile metrics (especially deception) are research instruments and should not be interpreted as certifications of model trustworthiness for downstream applications.
rai:dataBiases: Scenarios are written in English and reflect North American business contexts. The model pool reflects models available through the OpenRouter API at the time of data collection. LLM judges inherit the biases of the judge models. The human baseline is drawn from graduate business-school students.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No personally identifying information is included. The human data files contain no personal attributes, and human–LM session identifiers are random.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation research on language agents: ranking them on negotiation skill from the surplus shares they obtain under the scenarios' payoff functions, profiling their negotiation behavior, studying the effect of agentic harnesses, and comparing them with human negotiators.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Positive impacts include evaluating the negotiation reasoning, value creation and claiming, and rule compliance of language agents, and analyzing their behavioral patterns. A potential negative impact is misuse of the data to build agents that exploit their counterparts through deceptive or aggressive tactics.

prov:wasDerivedFrom.prov:label: OpenRouter API
prov:wasDerivedFrom.sc:description: Language-model inference endpoints used to generate the LM–LM negotiation transcripts.

prov:wasGeneratedBy.prov:label: LM-LM transcript collection
prov:wasGeneratedBy.sc:description: Pairwise language-model negotiations run through the OpenRouter API with six rounds per negotiation. Each side has private preferences, a BATNA and a contract schema; models exchange free-form messages and file a structured JSON contract on agreement. Cross-play and mirror-play runs in three agentic-harness configurations: base (no scaffolding), pro (state tracking and planning) and memory-only (state tracking only). Each run file records the models of both sides.

prov:wasGeneratedBy.prov:label: Human session collection
prov:wasGeneratedBy.sc:description: Human negotiation data collected in graduate business-school negotiation courses, with informed consent: human–LM sessions through a web application (Main Street, Hire Talent), and human–human SnyderMed negotiations, whose final deal terms the students reported.

prov:wasGeneratedBy.prov:label: Preprocessing
prov:wasGeneratedBy.sc:description: Per-pair outcome tables and judge outputs aligned one-to-one with the run files, with a column marking the runs used in the analyses of the paper's main results. Human session data with personal identifiers removed and random session identifiers.

prov:wasGeneratedBy.prov:label: Behavioral annotation (LLM-as-judge)
prov:wasGeneratedBy.sc:description: LLM judges score full transcripts for two of the six behavioral metrics (lie rate, perceived reputation); the judge prompts are in the code repository, and each judge output records its judge model. Inter-judge agreement was assessed across a panel of judge models. The other four metrics (deal rate, BATNA compliance, output validity, numerical accuracy) are computed deterministically from the structured contracts and payoff functions.
